title: Everyone talks of bliss
hook: everyone speaks of bliss, but bliss is known through the Guru (Anand 6)

segments.voice: Yesterday, pauri four, aadhaar, and your line, my support. Did you catch being satisfied by a little? Today, a pauri that asks what joy really is. Day three hundred eighty-six.

Search the word happiness in any bookstore and you'll get a wall. Ten steps to joy. The happiness project. How to be happy in thirty days. Apps that track your mood. Podcasts promising bliss by Friday. Everybody's selling it. Everybody's talking about it. And somehow the people talking about it most aren't always the people who seem to have it. The sixth pauri of Anand Sahib noticed the same thing, long before the first self-help shelf. It opens with an observation that could have been written this morning. Today: giaan anjan.
screen: `A WALL OF HAPPINESS BOOKS.` → `EVERYONE'S SELLING JOY.` → `FEW SEEM TO HAVE IT.`

segments.voice: The line, transliterated: anand anand sabh ko kahai, anand guroo te jaaniaa. Everyone speaks of bliss, bliss; but bliss is known through the Guru. Then, in paraphrase: true bliss is always known through the Guru, when the Beloved shows grace. By grace, wrongdoings are cut away, and the ointment of spiritual wisdom is put on the eyes. Those whose attachment has broken from within are made beautiful by the true Word. Says Nanak, this is bliss: bliss is known through the Guru. The image in the middle is worth stopping on. Giaan anjan, the ointment of wisdom. Anjan is the dark ointment people lined their eyes with. So the pauri pictures wisdom not as more information, but as something applied to your eyes, so you see differently. The world doesn't change. Your sight does. Then the key phrase: those whose attachment, moh, has broken from within. That's where the difference lies between the talk and the real thing. Much of the bliss on that bookstore wall is a new thing to grab: a purchase, a trip, a win. The pauri's bliss starts with letting go of the grabbing. It's known, the pauri says, through the Guru, as something received by grace and recognized from inside, not bought or argued into. And notice the word jaaniaa, known. Not felt for an afternoon. Known, the way you know your own front door. Sikhs don't say ordinary happiness is bad. A good meal, a good laugh, are gifts. The pauri just says there's a deeper joy, known through the Guru. Some readers put it simply: it doesn't leave when the afternoon does.
screen: `EVERYONE SPEAKS OF BLISS.` · `KNOWN THROUGH THE GURU.` · `GIAAN ANJAN: WISDOM ON THE EYES.` · `WHEN ATTACHMENT BREAKS WITHIN.` · then, large: `REAL JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what real joy felt like. Sit and breathe slowly. Think back to a moment of real joy in your life. Not excitement, not a win, but the quieter kind, the kind that stayed. Maybe holding a newborn, a moment in prayer, a long talk with someone you love, a sunrise you didn't expect. Let it come back. Notice where you feel it in your body. Notice what you weren't grabbing for at that moment. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you hold it. If you don't, just let yourself remember what real joy was like. The bell holds the time.
Giaan anjan, the ointment of wisdom. Everyone speaks of bliss, but bliss is known through the Guru, when attachment breaks within.
Your line: real joy. Today, when something makes you happy, ask quietly: is this the grabbing kind, or the kind that stays? Day three hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this sixth pauri as part of the full forty-pauri Anand Sahib in the morning Nitnem; its opening line is often quoted in Sikh teaching about the difference between pleasure and true bliss.

giaan anjan: the world doesn't change, your sight does.
pauri six is one of the six sung at every service's close
the short form is pauris one to five and forty; pauri six is in the full forty.

fork.setup: everyone around you is talking about bliss, and selling it too. what does pauri six say about where it's known?
options: bliss is known through the Guru.
fork.reveal: anand anand sabh ko kahai, anand guroo te jaaniaa: everyone speaks of bliss; bliss is known through the Guru, when attachment breaks within.

original.note: Gurmukhi: giaan anjan, the ointment of wisdom applied to the eyes, in Anand's sixth pauri.

trapdoor: what you thought: everyone wants to be happy.
what it means: everyone talks of bliss, but it's known through the Guru, when attachment breaks and wisdom clears the eyes.
what a scholar hears: anjan is the collyrium used to line and protect the eyes; gurbani often uses it as an image of spiritual wisdom changing the way one sees.
recall: the wicked, the one who means harm

sources.quoted: anand anand sabh ko kahai, anand guroo te jaaniaa

notes: Pauri 6 paraphrased ('jaaniaa anand sadaa gur te kirpaa kare piaariaa; kar kirpaa kilvikh kate giaan anjan saariaa; andarahu jin kaa moh tutaa tin kaa sabad sachai savaariaa'). Confirm.
'Over four hundred years before the first self-help shelf': Guru Amar Das lived 1479–1574; Anand Sahib is from the 16th century. Confirm phrasing.
Anjan (collyrium) and its use as an image in gurbani: confirm.
Pauri 6 is not part of the six-pauri short form (1–5, 40). Confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the 'four hundred years' count; trimmed the unsourced claim about anjan's purpose; the 'doesn't leave when the afternoon does' line is now a reader's gloss, not something the pauri says.
